state.misconception_label: Struggles to visualise nets of 3D shapes

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This is the net of a... ![A circle touching a sector](). I got Triangle because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are wrapping a present in the shape of a pyramid. Each face of the pyramid is like a side of the present, and when you unfold the wrapping paper, you'll see the net of the pyramid. The net of a triangular-based pyramid has a triangle for the base and three triangles for the sides. This visualization can help you understand how the 3D shape connects to its net.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so you unfold it like wrapping paper - that makes sense! But I'm still confused about my question though, because the picture I had showed a circle with a triangle bit next to it, not loads of triangles like you're describing. Is that a different shape then?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are cutting a slice of cake from a cylindrical cake. The circle represents the top view of the cake, and the triangle next to it is the side view of the slice you're cutting. Just like how the cake slice is part of the whole cake, the triangle is part of the net of a 3D shape called a cone. This analogy can help you see how different parts of a 3D shape's net come together.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, so it's a cone! That makes more sense now - so the circle is like the base of the cone and the triangle bit wraps around to make the pointy side? But I'm still a bit confused about how the triangle actually wraps around the circle - like, does the curved edge of the triangle match up with the edge of the circle or something?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides analogies rather than addressing the student's specific visualization struggles, gives answers directly rather than prompting reasoning, and while the student identifies the shape name by Turn 4, they still demonstrate confusion about how the net actually folds (asking about curved edges matching), suggesting the core misconception persists.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (wrapping presents, cutting cake slices) to explain abstract geometric concepts, which is a textbook implementation of the experiential strategy.
